It's June 25, 13:30 and the Grand Prix of Azerbaijan is about to start. Max Verstappen is on pole 5 and my wife is already in front of the TV looking at the warming up. 

Two days earlier I bought Firewatch which was already a long time on my Steam wishlist. I'm thinking to myself: "I'll play half an hour and then watch the Grand Prix." I start up my laptop on the kitchen table and start Firewatch and immediately get some very interesting and real life questions. One really hits me in the stomach and makes me wonder what kind of game poses these real life questions. 

Then the game begins. My wife calls that the start of the Grand Prix is almost about to broadcast. Reluctantly I get up and watch the start. Nothing special, so I get back to the game. I am completely mesmerized by the graphics, the voice acting is phenomenal and the story pulls me in completely. I am Henry and I am a Firewatch and my only radio contact is with Delilah. This is done so brilliantly that I forget everything around me. Although I am playing without a headset, somewhere far away I hear my wife yell: " That bloody Vettel just crashed his car deliberately into Hamilton's car, mother******!" Annoyed I watch the TV for a second, not even seeing what is happening as I already turn my head to my laptop screen again and play on. 

I walk through canyons and woods, solve puzzles, finish tasks Delilah gives to me and unravel the mystery behind the story. And that story is so intriguing that I keep playing and playing. This game is ART and easily one of the best games I ever played in my 45 years of gaming.

Five hours later I look up from the screen realizing that I finished it and my wife is in the garden. I didn't see her leave. 

Only on the eight 'o clock news I hear Daniel Ricciardo won the Grand Prix...

A simulator of spending hours flirting over the radio with your alcoholic boss while developing an absolutely insane conspiracy paranoia in the middle of nowhere, only for the game to remind you that your real adult life problems are still waiting for you back in the city. 10/10.

This review is an open letter to one of the developers, Jane Ng, the lead environmental artist at Campo Santo.

Jane recently made a very thoughtful post right here on the Steam Community Forums...

-----------

"hey there.

I thought about not responding, because normally ppl who want to refund are rude and unpleasant and I choose to not engage and dwell on it.

You seem nice and I figured what the heck, why not have a conversation about this, now that I have read it and it's right here in front of me.

So here is what I think. As the developer. Sorry if it's a bit stream of consciousness because I want this to come from the heart.

The 11 of us all took a lot of risk to make this, and sacrificed financially to give Firewatch a chance. We all could have had much better paying jobs elsewhere, but we all thought this game idea had potential to be something special. We seemed to like each other ok, so we all took a big leap of faith. Two years, we say. Let's give this a go, worst outcome is we all hate each other and go back to various money jobs, but we all could say, WE TRIED.

Two years +. We are all crammed in a tiny office, sharing one bathroom. It is not a glamorous thing, making an independent game. It is just a small room full of computers and a used microwave and $10 office chairs we luckily got from craigslist. Life happened during those two years: there were big breakups, profound illnesses of loved ones, a baby, etc. The dev team got to be like family, because that's how making an indie game is, you are all in it together, through thick and thin, supporting one another bc if you don't, there is no way in hell this game would get made, let alone any chance of it to be worth more than a bucket of ♥♥♥♥.

We were excited, but terrified. We felt free, but were constrained. I have been in this industry for 15 years almost, and this is the hardest I have ever worked. We all gave it our all, to make this weird thing, and we had no idea if it was any good to anybody else. All we could do, was try the damn hardest to make something we are honestly proud of. At the end, if this was a commercial failure, all we have got is what we have made. Nobody could take that away.

So yes, I am sad when people think this game is not worth the money we asked for (which we thought was a fair ask). It makes me feel like I failed them. It is ok if people don't like the game, but it affects me personally a lot, when people feel like it was not -worth- the time they engaged with it.

But do I blame you for wanting to get the most out of your $18? No. I don't know your financial circumstances. $18 might be a lot. Or even it isn't a lot, why shouldnt' you try to get the most out of it? That's a fair desire. That's why we asked for $18 too, because money is something we could all use more of.

So I supopse in conclusion, if you do refund, I am not upset. It's on me to learn not to care too much. All I ask is that maybe sometime in the future, when the game goes on mega dirt cheap sale, you could gift tthe experience to someone else you think will enjoy it like you did.

Sincerely,
Jane"

The price of videogames and the value you get out of them is often compared to going to the movies. You can spend 20 bucks on a 3D flick with some popcorn and a drink or use that to get a game of the same length or even more.
I think that deep down we still feel the need to justify the medium, even though I understand the argument, but Firewatch was the first title that made me reconsider that comparison and where it immediately made sense to me.

Firewatch is a [i]walking simulator[/i], with Telltale-esque dialogues, that tells the story of a man that chose escapism as his life went downhill and became a fire lookout. 
The prologue is only told with text and some accompanying soundscapes, but I already felt deeply moved and instantly invested in the story, which tells a lot about the writing, where other games struggle to achieve this level of immersion even with access to all the artistic tools videogames offer.

As soon as you're thrown into the actual game you can't help but be amazed by the breathtaking vistas and goregeous color pallets. Definitely one of the most beautiful games I've ever laid eyes on.
The story itself is mostly conveyed with dialogues between the protagonist and his superior via walkie talkie and the voice acting is on par with big budget productions, if not better, and again the writing proves its quality. 

Those 4 hours I've played were incredibly dense and intense. [i]All killer, no filler[/i]. It's an emotional rollercoaster.

Yes, the game is short and yes, the game costs a bit much, considering you can get more bang for your buck these days, but I don't think I have ever played such a compelling game. 
And if this wouldn't have been a christmas gift I probably would've waited for a steep discount, yet after finishing the game I think that those 20 dollars are more than justified. Just like going to the movies.

Firewatch is a unique & interesting game. The game is so unique that it’s unlike anything I’ve played & the game does not fit neatly into any one genre. I would describe Firewatch as an interactive movie, walking simulator, suspense game. One playthrough of Firewatch took me roughly 9 hrs. But I play games slowly, so a typical gamer could finish the game in perhaps 4-5 hours.

 Firewatch is polished & high quality. The game has a good frame rate & quality, smooth gameplay. Moreover, the game offers intuitive & responsive controls. Also, the game is easy yet not boring or shallow. And, the game’s art design is stylized. It’s eye-catching & interesting, looking like a realistic painting.

Firewatch boasts some of the best voice acting I’ve heard in a game. The performances are believable & compelling. The stellar voice acting carries the game; the phenomenal voice acting makes the game stand out, given that a major part of the game are the conversations by radio the MC has with Delilah. Since you never see Delilah, the voice acting does the heavy lifting.

Let’s discuss the game’s ending without spoilers. Many people don’t like the ending. To be fair, the ending is straightforward & anticlimactic. But the ending is also surprising, shocking & profound. To me this shows the genius of the developers. I ended up liking the ending once I understood it (I had to Google it as the ending’s meaning is profound & hard to see). I loved that I came away from the game with such thought-provoking & deep commentary on the human condition.

Firewatch does have some flaws. The biggest flaw is the mediocre & disappointing free-roam mode. After you beat the game, you can free roam the beautiful game world. But you don’t keep the tools you gained from beating the game. Hence, large parts of the game world are unavailable for free roam. This was a huge disappointment for me.

Another flaw, although minor, is that the game does not have auto-walk or auto-run. So you have to manually walk & run. Thankfully, the game map is not huge. Even still, it was annoying & rather tedious to have to constantly hold the movement buttons.

Another minor flaw is that in one aspect, the game suffers from a lack of realism. The game takes place in a forest, yet there are almost no animals. This is unrealistic. Just realize that Firewatch is not an animal-watching game.

Finally, despite the game's name, you never actually do any fire watching. Instead, you do a lot of hiking. Personally, this flaw did not bother me because I wanted a hiking simulator game. But I could easily see this flaw bothering some players, maybe many.

In conclusion, Firewatch is a prime example of video games as art. It’s amazing to see what the video game medium can produce. I highly recommend Firewatch, especially if you’re looking for something unique & want a memorable experience. I know I’ll be thinking about this game for a long time.

Firewatch is a quiet mystery for gamers who know how to listen. A strong script and exceptional dialogue direction make Firewatch to one of the best interactive storytelling experiences you can get your hands on.

Firewatch is a game about people. Not exaggerated or broken characters just ordinary individuals dealing with the weight of their own lives. At its heart, the game is about escape the ways people run from responsibility, grief, or emotional strain, and how those attempts to disconnect can reveal more about them than the problems they’re avoiding. You play as someone who retreats into the quiet isolation of the Wyoming wilderness, and the game leans into that feeling of getting away from everything. The routine tasks, the long walks, the small disturbances in the forest they’re intentionally mundane, grounding you in a space that feels both peaceful and lonely. The real emotional pull comes from the relationship that develops over the radio. The conversations are thoughtful, vulnerable, often surprisingly honest, and they gradually reveal how both characters are using this distance to confront or avoid their own issues. The dialogue is the soul of the game, turning simple exchanges into meaningful moments.

One of Firewatch’s strengths is how it blends this personal connection with a sense of unease that slowly builds in the background. The game never relies on big twists or dramatic reveals instead, it focuses on the tension that comes from uncertainty, isolation, and not fully understanding what’s happening around you. It uses atmosphere, sound, and the environment to keep you on edge without ever breaking the grounded, human tone of the story. By the time the journey reaches its end, Firewatch doesn’t try to provide a clean moral or a neatly wrapped conclusion. Instead, it reflects the messy way life often unfolds where closure isn’t guaranteed, and where people sometimes leave things unresolved because they don’t know how to face them. Ultimately, Firewatch is less about mystery and more about the emotional landscapes people carry with them. It’s a quiet, immersive experience that sticks with you not because of what happens, but because of why people do the things they do.

Firewatch is not for everyone, but I did greatly enjoy it. A game that I didn't quite understand when I first finished it, but after thinking about it a great deal, I think I understand it's purpose. 

It is incredibly well written and every detail matters, just not in the way you think it will. Every character and line of dialogue is purposeful and, when it's all said and done, makes a very real and interesting point about how we as humans tend to deal with life's hardships. 

My interpretation:
*SPOILERS*
I think this game's purpose was to show that some people choose NOT to deal with their problems at all. Henry and Dililah try to escape their mistakes and their real-life problems. Henry is unable to properly care for his sick wife. He goes out drinking in order to escape his responsibilities. Eventually Julia's family takes her in to care for her. Henry takes the firewatch job to escape his failure and the pain that comes with his wife having dementia. 
Dililah got dumped by her long-time boyfriend because she couldn't be there for him when his family member died. She works out in the forest every summer to escape her mistakes. Throughout the game it is made known that she also uses alcohol as an escape, just like Henry often does. Alcohol is a reoccuring symbol of attempted escape. Even the teenage girls use alcohol to try to escape. But in every case, it never works. 
Henry and Dililah spend most of the game pursuing answers to what seems to be a conspiracy. This also serves as an escape. They keep finding clues and it leads them to assume more and more dramatic possibilities. Is the government watching them? Are they being studied or set up? In the end it is just Ned, another character who is escaping his responsibilities. He caused his son's death, and chooses to hide in the woods instead of face what he's done and give his son a proper barial. He was only trying to keep henry from finding his son's body. 
Dililah is also an escape for Henry, and vice versa. They sort of fancy each other and flirt quite a bit. You even find Henry has removed his wedding ring and set it on the table at one point. They use each other as escapes from their own romantic issues.
Even the fire is a symbol. Dililah talks about how last year the authorities thought they could let the wild fire runs its course. No. She says Yellowstone almost burned down. You can't ignore fire (the problem), it will only spread and do more damage. The deer Henry sees in the beginning of the game flees just like he did. The teenagers steal a tractor and go to jail, they were running from their problems. Julia and Henry choose to take a different path for walking the dog after they almost got robbed. 
The point of all this is that every attempt at escape fails. There is no conspiracy, all the clues lead to nothing. Just coincidental occurences, and Ned trying to cover his tracks. Dililah tells Henry to go see his wife in the end. She knows they can't be together, and that he should face his responsiblity: Julia. 
I know a lot of people might think the end is disappointing. No conspiracy, no romance. But that's the point. That's life. You can't fix things by running away. There was no big twist or secret, just Henry and D letting their imaginations run wild. Trying to ignore their responsibilities. It is simply a very honest, real human tragedy.

Firewatch is a thought-provoking game that explores the human experience in a poignant and introspective way. While it may not be for everyone, the negative reviews I've seen miss the mark. This game isn't meant to be action-packed or filled with traditional gameplay mechanics. Instead, it's a slow-burning narrative that reflects on life in a somber manner, delving into themes of isolation, regret, and human connection. The stunning Wyoming wilderness serves as a hauntingly beautiful backdrop to the protagonist's emotional journey. The graphics and soundtrack are masterfully crafted, enhancing the immersive experience. If you're open to a game that prompts self-reflection and evokes deep emotions, Firewatch is a gem that deserves a perfect 10 out of 10 rating.

[strike]Firwatch[/strike] Firewatch is an enjoyable "first-person mystery" by a small team of folks who know what they are doing.

Applying the "walking simulator" is not inaccurate, but that may be too dismissive of the refined experience Firewatch offers.

Much walking through a nicely realized, highly stylized forest environment is involved, but the most notable ingredient of the game is your character's interaction with the other main character via portable radio - one of the finer examples of such interaction in the video game medium.

The game starts by building a backstory of your character via text, allowing you to make several choices - an effective technique to help you identify with your character. These choices are later reflected in dialogue (although they do not, as far as I know, have a significant impact on the plot). The dialogue mechanic, the control over dialogue responses effectively facilitates immersion and the dialogue is very well voiced.

Firewatch does a good job at pacing, at maintaining suspense. Although, you can choose at times to wander off on a few detours and delay story progression. There's a decent amount of optional secrets and details to discover, but not very many - if short on time, don't worry about them and just stick to the goals at hand, as you won't miss much. The game can last about 4-8 hours depending on how much you stray/dawdle.

Perhaps the most questionable aspect of the game is the hype and marketing that emphasizes the mystery. There certainly is mystery, and it's pretty good, but many, perhaps even most, might be surprised and perhaps disappointed that the story progression doesn't match quite the expectations they had. Although I did feel a mild sense of being the victim of misdirection, I liked the story, and the game.

The other perhaps surprising but astute design principle here is what isn't explicitly shown. The (visual and auditory) presentation is such that much is left to the imagination and exposition is trickle-fed. A cynic might accuse this paradigm of being a cost saving measure. And maybe it is. But, it is effective at engaging the player's mind.

I recommend Firewatch as a short but good interactive mystery experience, especially if it's on sale.
Yes, it's a narrative-driven experience. Yes, it's a "walking simulator." Sometimes those games are good too. This is one.

* it's not very long with only 4-5hrs gameplay tops
* your decisions/dialogue options have only minor impact on the story. There are some very neat responds to what you do (i.e. if you take the wiskey bottle, the dialog responds to that later), but no real game-changing events

[h1]But I still really recommend it because...[/h1]
* the stile is very unique (in a positive way, "art")
* the dialogue varies between very deep thoughts and quite funny jokes
* the story and both protagonists could really be like this in the real world
* albeit it's pretty short, I have more memories about it than to any shooter or many other games

Firewatch is one of those games that quietly wrecks you. You go in thinking it’s just a walking sim, trees, sunsets, and then suddenly you're knee-deep in your own feelings because a woman on the radio asked how you're holding up.

There’s no combat, no inventory. Just you, a damaged past, and Delilah’s voice in your ear. And somehow… that’s enough. More than enough.

Short game. Long aftertaste.
See you, Delilah. Maybe in another life.

Firewatch is an adventure game, developed and published by Campo Santo that was released in February 2016 on PC.  The core team behind this game have got a plethora of experience, with some coming from big titles such as Mark of the Ninja, Brutal Legend and Bioshock 2 so I went into this game with high expectations. 

You play as a middle aged man named Henry, whose wife has sadly got dementia, a crippling illness which tears people’s lives apart. Doing what a lot of people do in this world, Henry runs away from his problems to become a woodland ranger in a national forest. Your job is to mainly look out for signs of a fire in the dry woodlands and help prevent them spreading across the rest of the forest.  This should be a calm and relaxing job for most, but you soon become the centre of a massive conspiracy plot as the story unravels. 

Gameplay consists of hiking across rough terrain in order to reach objective points, loot supply crates which contain key game play tools such as ropes or walkie-talkies as well as notes left by past rangers which form part of the history of the park and give you some back plot to the story.   Another core element to this game is the interaction you have with the only other human you have contact with throughout, Delilah – you maintain contact with her through your radio and talk to her every day. The two develop a relationship depending on how you respond to her in dialog and actions throughout the story.  The dialog was probably the most compelling part of this game; the hiking between objectives did actually grow a little tiresome at times and grew very repetitive towards the end of the game. 

The story is what carries this game hands down, I’ve been on a bit of an adventure game binge lately and this is by far the most interesting and gripping story I’ve played in recent memory. The relationship and bond between the main character Henry and Deliaha develops throughout the game and you really find yourself becoming completely immersed in this story. The game will leave you asking yourself moral questions too, and of course the ending will allow you to decide yourself on how everything works out in the end. You’ll probably finish the game with more questions than answers, and normally that would point to a case of bad storytelling, but in this case it is simply amazing that a story such as this can bring out so many emotions and questions regarding certain subjects. 

Whilst the game isn’t the most graphically enhanced, it does have a nice art style that is pleasing to the eye. The game is ran using the Unity engine so we do get OK looking graphics but some of the texture quality and graphical effects are lacking which let Firewatch down sadly. The voice acting and sound effects are all really good though, again the dialog between characters is spot on and I cannot fault it even for one second in that department. 

The forest in which you are situated is huge, although the game has set objectives throughout the story, you are allowed to roam around and explore anything you want. You will come across certain areas of the map that you can’t explore just yet as you won’t have the right equipment, such as axes or climbing gear, but you are free to check out every nut and granny if you please. You will find a handful of those supply crates I spoke about above scattered around the forest, along with a few points of interest too. 

Due to the fairly linear overall story line there may not be room for more than two playthroughs of the game; yes you can choose to respond differently to Deliaha and that will result in different dialog between the two characters but I personally don’t see any other reason other than achievement hunting – to play more than twice. A single play through of Firewatch took me just over five hours to complete. 

I had minor technical issues whilst playing, you will get some stuttering when you enter a more graphically heavy area such as near a large mass of water, or looking over a cliff with a long draw distance; I was a little disappointed in this as my rig is more than capable of playing this game on high settings according to the specs recommended. I was able to get a little bit of a performance boost by using an SLI profile for my graphics card and thankfully was able to get a steady 60 FPS with the odd stutter throughout my time playing. I did also fall through the world a number of times which did become a huge annoyance as it kept repeatedly happening but this was fixed by reloading the game. 

My conclusion of Firewatch is that it a stellar adventure game, which whilst it does have faults with average looking special graphical effects and minor technical problems; it is still a joy to play through. The story kept me gripped right until the end, and the relationships that you form between the two characters are brilliantly executed.  The price tag of £14.99 is completely fair and justified given the production values on offer for this title. The game has very rarely been on sale up until now so we might get a heavy discount in the upcoming Steam sale, so keep your eyes peeled.

Halfway through playing the game I searched for reviews, and found people describing the ending as underwhelming. I didn't quite understand why — not even after unlocking all the achievements — until I finally realized that the game's mainstream appeal lies in Henry and Delilah developing an emotional connection. What disappointed people was precisely the fact that Henry and Delilah never meet. Looking back, I awkwardly remembered that I never shared anything about Julia with Delilah throughout the game, deflected her flirtatious remarks, and played deaf to her teasing. And then it struck me — I related far more to Ned, who knew deep down he had made terrible mistakes yet was too cowardly to face reality; and to Dave, who carried emotions as deep and heavy as the ocean but kept a calm facade just to keep life moving.  
I was drawn to this game because ChatGPT recommended it as "a space for awake eyes and ears beyond the numbness of reality". In the end, it reminded me of how much of a mess my own emotional world still is, how my choice to seal off my emotions from others and painstakingly construct a solitary inner world remains unconventional, even alien. The only solace I found was that, during the fleeting hours I spent wandering the rocky trails and caves, I felt a solid, unspeakable emotional connection with the lonely souls of Shoshone National Forest, and with all the players who had ever been comforted by this game. And that, I realized, was enough. Henry leaving the Wyoming wilderness still has to return to a world revolving around his wife with dementia; Ned, exposed and forced out of his solitary life, likely faces an uphill struggle to find his next psychological sanctuary; and we, shutting off the game and returning to our daily lives, will once again grind away our patience in the 9-5 monotony until we grow weary and wither. The game and life share the same theme: brief escapes are always followed by the inescapable force of long separations. Fate listens to neither your explanations nor your pleas — it just moves forward. Yet, on some random warm spring Saturday nights, we might find ourselves thinking about these kind smiles and gentle people, these books, these songs, these games that remind us we are not alone and we can still find noble souls to talk to: tiny, fragile beams of light that, in the prolonged darkness of life, illuminate our path. I'm grateful for and deeply admire this kind of light.

Loneliness, Pine Trees, and the Woman in My Ear

Firewatch is the kind of game that sneaks up on you. One minute you’re hiking through the Wyoming wilderness in your ranger-issued shorts, trying to figure out how a couple of drunk teens managed to set half the forest on fire with fireworks, and the next you're emotionally spiraling because a woman with a devastatingly sexy voice on the radio asked how you're really doing.

This isn’t a shooty-bang-bang game. There are no dragons. No inventory management. No high-octane car chases. Just you, the wilderness, a walkie-talkie, and a job watching for fire. Sounds boring, right? It’s not. It’s haunting. It’s funny. It’s beautiful. And somehow, it becomes one of the most intimate games I’ve ever played.

You play as Henry, a man who took a job in the middle of nowhere to escape his own wreckage of a life. The setup is simple: you sit in a tower, spot fires, report back. But what makes this game burn is Delilah—your supervisor, your only friend, and the woman whose voice slowly becomes your entire emotional support system.

And that voice? Delilah’s voice is dangerous.

Sultry, sarcastic, warm, and wounded—every time she speaks, it’s like whiskey being poured over an old wound. I found myself hiking through brush, not to complete an objective, but just to get to the next conversation. She’s flirty. She’s funny. She’s human. And somehow, you fall in love—not with her face, not with her body (you never even see her), but with the idea of her. With the sound of her. With the company of her.

Firewatch is brilliant in that way. It lets you fall for someone using nothing but a voice and a radio signal. And when the world starts unraveling around you—mystery, paranoia, fire closing in—Delilah is your anchor… even when you’re not sure if you can trust her.

Gameplay-wise, it’s a walking sim, yes. You walk. You talk. You occasionally climb rocks and swat away branches like a sweaty philosopher. But the real journey is internal. It’s about grief, connection, and what it means to be seen by someone, even if they’re hundreds of miles away.

The art style? Gorgeous. Like an oil painting of the American West lit on fire at golden hour. The soundtrack? Sparse and perfect. The story? Quietly devastating. No big plot twists. No happy endings. Just real, raw emotion wrapped in pine needles and smoke.

Final verdict? Firewatch is a short game with long echoes. It’s about healing, about escape, about two broken people clinging to each other through static. I didn’t want to leave that tower. I didn’t want to lose that voice in my ear. And when the game ended, I sat in silence and wondered how a voice I never saw could feel more real than half the characters in my life.

So here’s to Delilah. Wherever you are, radio girl… I still think about you.

First off, let's get it out of the way and say that yes, the game is extremely short. It took me about three hours to play all the way through the story. With no incentive to replay it, the game might not be worth the asking price for many people who read this review. If you don't want to pay $20 for a 3 hour experience, then that is fine, and respectable.

However, the experience that you're buying here is something unlike other games you've played. Firewatch, no matter what all the naysayers believe, is a very groundbreaking game. It did something no other game has ever done for me: make me feel like I was talking to an actual human being when I had conversations with Delilah as Henry. The connection you build with her is something unlike anything you'll see in another game. It just feels so... real. She feels like a real person. I believe that the feeling is amplified by the fact that you never really see a physical representation of Delilah in the game. You only ever speak to her through your handy walkie-talkie, which means the only thing I ever associated her with, was with a real, breathing human.

The story that Firewatch tells is also an extremely believable, heart-wrenching, and yet heart-warming one. I'll not go into details or spoilers, but let's just say that the story is a very human mystery, and has a few twists that leave you pondering every single thing you ever did in the game, and wondering how it was all connected. The story wasn't something that will completely blow your mind and make you rethink your life, but it is just that hint of subtlety that makes it so enjoyable. It just feels so real, man.

I believe that the price tag on Firewatch is worthwhile. The beauty of the landscape in which the game is set isn't really comparable to very many other games. The world is exquisitely detailed, and the art style does a lot for the overall atmosphere the game is going for. Photorealism wasn't something that the developers were going for, as the art has a very cartoonish, animated feeling - and yet all of the finer details in the world are still there, such as print on the back of some of the books found in the game that can actually be read. The environment will immerse you in your surroundings, and if not for your map and compass and Delilah's guidance, it would be quite easy to get lost in the extensive wilderness in which the game is set. On top of that, the voice acting in the game is probably some of the best you'll ever hear. For such a small title, it is astonishing how well voice acted it was. The voice acting certainly helped to add to the immersion of the world, but it also helps justify the price of the title, as quality like that can't come cheap.

In the end, if you're looking for a quick, hearty game that you want to make you feel something, then this game is definitely worth your time, and your money. If you don't have the cash to fork out for a game you'll probably only ever play once, then I don't think this title is for you.

[h2]Firewatch: A Relationship Simulator[/h2]

My girlfriend and I played "Firewatch" as a couples' activity - except with less hiking and more dialogue. The game is designed for adults, not because of its mature content (although there is some of that), but because it understands relationships better than most games.

Every dialogue choice in the game felt like a test of how we respond in real life. Should we deflect with humor or admit our fears? Should we pretend to know something we don't? Seeing our partner choose different answers was like peeking into another world where people think before they speak.

The graphics are stunning, the music is perfect for creating mood, and the story is a slow build that leaves you wondering after the end. It's about escaping from problems and guilt, only to realize that we can't run away from our past.

Play it alone for self-reflection, or with a friend to see how you handle emotional vulnerability. Regardless of how you play it, this game is a masterpiece that shows how the most dangerous place can be between two people.

[i] (Please talk to each other and be honest with yourself and your partner. Live your life consciously, choosing not out of fear or according to your parents' expectations, but because it's what you really want. Trust in yourself, others and make decisions based on your own values and beliefs.) [/i]

These days I tend to enjoy games that are similar to a good book: a solitary, escapist experience I can get completely lost in without any interruptions from the outside world. Firewatch, then – on the strength of its gripping story, brilliant branching script, wholly convincing voice-acting performances, and stunning art direction – is easily one of my favorite and most memorable game experiences of this decade.
Firewatch quickly lets you know that it’s not going to pull any emotional punches over its four to five–hour runtime, opening with a series of text-based choices that call back to adventure genre forebears like Zork. I dare not spoil this potent sequence, but I will say that it masterfully bounces between being funny and heart-wrenching and plausibly establishes just why protagonist Henry ends up in the Wyoming woods as a solitary fire lookout.

As a huge Valve and Half-Life: Alyx fan, I deemed it necessary to check this game out after hearing the involvement of Campo Santo in that title. And I must say, this game surprised me in unexpected ways: 

- The writing and voice acting is super high quality, and I grew to like both main characters very quickly [spoiler] despite all of their development being delivered through dialogue and text only; there are no traditional cutscenes where you see the characters moving, so this is a seriously impressive feat. [/spoiler]

- While the world has a slightly cartoony aesthetic, it feels very realistic and successfully creates an uplifting or tense atmosphere where appropriate, [spoiler] even though there is no combat whatsoever. [/spoiler]

- The narrative is really clever and successfully subverts the player’s expectations without feeling cheap; [spoiler] you feel like something bigger is going on as you would normally expect in video games, but the game decides to simply not go down that route. I think this is such a simple yet effective choice that makes it stand out by, well, not being bombastic in presentation like many other games would do. [/spoiler] 

- Like many people, the ending really confused me initially, but after sitting with it, it completely made sense given the direction of the narrative. [spoiler] I think the fact that many people seemed disappointed with it showed that the developers pulled off their vision successfully; we all expected something more substantial to happen, but the game’s final message reminds you of the harsh reality of the world, and that running from one’s problems can only last so long before it’s time to snap back to reality. [/spoiler]I understand why people wouldn’t like it, but at the end of the day, Firewatch is not particularly long so I don’t think it could really be said that it wasted anyone’s time, unless they completely despise walking simulators.

The game took me around three hours to beat, though if I was better with following the map and searching the environment in a couple of cases, this probably could have clocked in at about two and a half hours. This would be longer if you decide to not jog your way through the world, but I decided to do so throughout since the narrative consistently gripped me and I wanted to uncover the mystery surrounding it in good time. 

The game also offers free-roam after you beat the story, and there are a couple of extra achievements to track down if you want to squeeze the game for all its content, but aside from that there isn’t really much to do. It’s worth it at 75% off for sure, but due to its length I couldn’t really recommend it for anything above that since there isn’t much to do aside from the narrative. However, what is here is incredibly quality, and I’ll likely have this in mind when drawing up a list of my favourite games I played this year. 9/10.

While I have to say that I enjoyed this game and it was an endearing experience, I can't really recommend this game due to the fact that I don't feel like I enjoyed it any more than I would've just watching a playthrough on YouTube. The characters are well written and relatable, the scenery looks nice and pretty, and the story starts off kinda nicely. But any decisions you make have extremely little if any real effect in-game, making different playthroughs essentially identical. 

While the setting looks nice and soothing it also lacks any real 'soul', there's not much exploration, and I feel like that wastes the map design. Wherever you go you're running into trees and rocks you can't cross, paths that go all over the place, and all of that only really serves to get the player lost and maybe extend the playtime a bit, making the player resort to pulling up the rather clunky map system every 10 steps. There's nothing much to see in this game aside from the trees and rivers, etc., and the game suffers from the gameplay consisting entirely of "Go from Point A to Point B". While this is a "Walking Simulator" as you might've heard, the game really relies on okay-scenery and occasional funny banter between the characters to keep you from falling asleep. 

The story also eventually devolves into a "mystery" kind of ordeal, which seems like a rather sharp turn from the tone of the game before. Not only does this "mystery" kind f come outta left field, it also lacks a satisfying conclusion, much ike the game itself. The ending is agreed upon by many to be rather disappointing, which some argue is on purpose, leaving the player empty and wanting more in some kind of artsy way. 

Another thing to take note of is the pricetag to playtime ratio here. There are games out there worth $10 that could keep you playing for dozens of hours. This game, however, falls a little short in that respect. It carries a heavy $20 pricetag despite the fact that players will not take more than 3-6 hours to finish this game, depending on how often and how badly they get lost. With different choices and options making really marginal difference, it causes this game to have EXTREMELY little replay value. In fact, the first minutes of the game are you making 'decisions' (as many are you just clicking from single dialogue option to progress), with the whole section having such little impact that it could've just as easily all been a textbox and the game is simply trying to fool you into thinking it's anything different. I can't in good conscience recommend a game of this price when it lacks so much in the entertainment value. 

I say you should only consider purchasing this game if you feel strongly about supporting the developers, and even then you should wait for a sale to come around.

I didn't think the story had a big reveal at the end, but the point of gettnig there to the end had me seriously at the edge of my seat at times. If you like immersive adventures with slowly unfolding stories which let you explore the game at your own pace, this is one you should definitely give a try!

[h1][b]Firewatch		* 9/10[/b][/h1]

Alone in a watchtower, guarding the forest and the entire park for fires and troubles. A quiet work, appearently, until odd things start to happen.

[h1][i]INTRO. What is Firewatch about?[/i][/h1]
It's 1989, you're Henry and you've just reached the watchtower of this park. You will be alone watching over the forest and your only human contact is Delilah, your supervisor that will give you tasks and advices. Job starts quietly with small trips from point to point, some nice chat with your boss and so on, but soon you will witness odd events and notthing will be the same.

Sounds generic, I know, but you will get to know Henry a lot more than it sounds, understanding the reason that brought him to this hermit life, the only human relation you're about to have will grow and evolve, and what you are about to see will involve you, make you suspicious, paranoid and worried. A story that seems incredible but not impossible.

[h1][i]GRAPHIC. Engine And Artistic aspects.[/i][/h1]
Made with Unity, the map (the park) is quite big, but you will obtain the necessary tools to reach all places along with your playthrough. The aspect is almost ALMOST cartoonish, with simple textures but no cel shading, yet the landscapes and places are simply marvelous. A canyon, a lake, planes, caves, the forest, everything is worth admiring for a second even though textures are quite essential. Locations have been realized with great care for details resulting in the beautiful park you can walk in.

[h1][i]SOUNDTRACK. Themes and Accompaniments.[/i][/h1]
You will rarely hear music during the game, but what you hear is simple yet very effective, simple movements, some classic guitar. Few tunes only during the right moments. Gives a stronger sense of loneliness walking through the park without hearing anything but nature and your own steps.

[h1][i]GAMEPLAY. How does it work?[/i][/h1]
Walking simulator. Nuff said. First person, you walk around, you can interact with specific objects and you can pick up a handful of items to use around in different specific occasions. The most interesting part however is the radio. You have a radio to communicate with Delilah. Sometimes she'll call you and lots of time you can call her... Mainly to report things and objects you find or need help with. And you can speak with her, chosing answers, or sentences according to the tone you want to use or the matter you want to talk about. In this lone place it's natural to be willing to speak with Delilah about as many things as you can. And it's made on purpose...

[h1][i]LAST NOTES. What doesn't work?[/i][/h1]
Nothing I guess. Unless you're looking for action but then I'd be surprised you're giving attention to a Walking simulator.

[h1][i]TL;DR. Pros And Cons[/i][/h1]

[*][b] THE PARK.[/b] It's, simply put, beautiful. There are Wonderful environments and landscapes to see and the paradox is that textures are so simple and almost cartoonish.

And someone who finds comfort in the presence of another broken person, someone who is willing to listen and someone who understands what it's like to run away from your past, your bad choices and feeling lost in life.
Spending this summer with Henry and Delilah, listening to their conversations, learning what kind of people they are and what brought them to Wyoming and investigating the strange happenings in the national park, everything just a coincidence in these two people's lives. 
They are more human than I'd like to admit and their troubles seem so real that you really feel for them and at times find yourself enjoying the moments of peace and quiet while hiking through the park, briefly leaving the heavyness of it all behind you and just taking in the view, getting lost in the colors.

You're faced with some tough choices in this game, I found myself second guessing my own choices later on, questioning if there would've been a better way to do things, a better way to react to certain questions and situations, something I missed, something I overlooked. In the end, it doesn't really matter because when I made the choices they seemed right.

Firewatch (FW) is a first-person adventure game set in the wilderness of a forest. Part open-world, part walking simulator, it is a slow-burn story that focused on creating an emotional journey for the player. Does it succeed in this regard? Let’s dive in.

[h2]Pros[/h2]
- Beautifully-rendered woodland environments 
- Complex characters with excellent voice acting
- A branching narrative to create your own journey
- Engaging story filled with mysteries

[h2]Cons[/h2]
- The ending 

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
As mentioned above, FW is a unique mix of two genres. It is still mainly a walking simulator with a couple of action sequences sprinkled in. However, the places that you need to go are often far away from your starting area and you are only given vague directions on how to get there. Thus, you are provided with a map that covers all notable places with proper legends. As you progressed through the game, it will be gradually filled with more useful tidbits such as notable landmarks, hidden shortcuts or blocked paths. A thing to note here is that the map is a physical object, meaning you have to regularly consult it (with the help of a compass) to find your way around. There is no heads-up display, minimap or anything similar. This contributes to making the game feel more immersive, much like you would be hiking in real life.

If you are seeking for a game to spice up your computer’s screensaver, look no further. Every single scene in FW is jaw-dropping to look at, especially during sundown. The locations that you ventured into also varied frequently, from the luscious forest to a wide canyon to a gloomy cave. Clearly, a lot of effort is put into creating a life-like world full of amazing discoveries.

Speaking of discoveries, the details put into the environments are spectacular. Contrary to most walking simulators, almost every object can be picked up and inspected closely. For a clear-cut example, there are more than a dozen books hidden around the wilderness and all of them have their specialized cover and even a readable synopsis on the back. 

[h2]Story[/h2]
Our journey begins from the perspective of Henry (Rich Sommer), an everyday man that chose to work as a fire lookout in the Wyoming jungle to escape his troubled life. Being stranded in the middle of nowhere, his only form of socialization is with his superior, Delilah (Cissy Jones) using a small handheld radio. The job is simple: keep watch for any potential fire while making sure everything is nice and cozy. Seems like a walk in the park, right? Or so he thought.

These two characters ooze personality from the very beginning. Even though we never get to physically interact with Delilah, the conversations that we can engage with her are believable and three-dimensional. Not once do I feel that both of them are flat, uninteresting individuals; instead, I wanted to learn more about them. This is greatly helped by the voice actors who pour their strengths into bringing these people to life.

I would like to acknowledge the theme here, which I believe to be about relationships and isolation (while keeping the spoilers to a minimum). Henry’s broken past heavily involved a close bond and he used the job as a way to cope in silence. Apart from that, some of his talks with Delilah are about their former lives and what it means to care for someone. You can also find a couple of leftover notes detailing the relationship between two former lookouts; hell, even one of the books is about ‘the untapped power of the solitary mind’. It is a thought-provoking subject matter that the writers manage to present fairly well for the most part.

Using the radio, you can inform Delilah of any point of interest that you may have stumbled upon, and these are presented in the form of dialogue trees. These not only encouraged me to explore any secrets FW has to offer, but also expands their relationship further. While the responses that you chose will not affect the events that follow, it does impact Henry’s attitude and his overall stand with his supervisor. Therefore, the destination may be the same, but the journey will be personalized to each player.

And while we are on that topic, let’s discuss the destination AKA the ending. Truth be told, I do not like it. Not in the sense that it was despicable, but because it was a letdown. While it does explain all of the events you witnessed throughout the game, the answers are simply underwhelming (albeit realistic).

[h1]The Rest[/h1]
[list]
[*] Developers Commentary is available from the start if you are interested in learning the behind-the-scenes of FW.
[*] After completing the game once, a Free Roam mode is available where you can explore the entire map to your heart’s content. The only downside is Delilah is unavailable to talk to.
[*] You can find and pet a turtle. Truly the mark of a next-gen game.
[/list]

[h1]Stats[/h1]
[b]Playtime:[/b] It took me eight hours to complete FW, getting all achievements in the process. 

[b]Replayability:[/b] Minimal. Free Roam can be fun, but by that point, you probably uncovered everything.

[b]Achievements:[/b] Ten of them, which means ten percent per achievement. All of them are a piece of cake to obtain.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]
Campo Santo’s debut game is anything but forgettable. With a simple premise, basic gameplay and minimal characters, they successfully created one of the most memorable walking simulators to date. It is not an experience you want to miss. All in all, I recommend Firewatch.

I may have lost my way more than once because I absolutely suck at navigating, but the breathtaking vista's and goregeous color pallets more than made up for that.

The ending left me a bit unsatisfied, but I absolutely recommend this game for the story, dialogue and amazing atmosphere.

Firewatch is a game whee you play as a man named Henry. Your wife Julia is sick with Dementia and moves back to Australia. You want to escape from everything and you decide to become a volunteer and become a firewatcher. When you arrive at your outpost you meet a woman named Delilah who is gonna be the only person you talk to through the entire game. You never see her and the only way to talk to her is through your trusty radio. The game also has a sub plot, but I'll cover that a bit tad later.

The dialogue between Henry and Delilah is my favorite part of the game. It feels very natural how they talk between each other and I feel like that helps a lot with the game. 

Firewatch is a walking simulator and a very bare bones one at that. The game takes place over a period of 79 days ( you don't play through all of them) where you explore the forest. When you explore the forest you can sometimes find stuff that have an icon of a radio next to them and you can talk about that stuff to Delilah and maybe spark up a conversation that will reveal the more about Delilah or Henry. The game also lets you explore the entire map at your own pace, so if you want to wander off and explore you are free to do so, but Delilah will drop in once in a while to remind you what you're supposed to be doing.

The graphics are absolutely outstanding. The entire environment looks absolutely gorgeous and it's breathtaking just to go to the highest point in the map and look around at the sights which are all just amazing. The entire forest feels alive as the trees sway with the wind and the sounds of the wilderness help to build the perfect atmosphere.

The soundtrack is also amazing, when you explore the music sometimes changes to somber music to stuff that will creep you out a bit, it's all very good and definitely worth owning the soundtrack.

Alright now I'm going to the territory of stuff that I thought were really bizarre and downright poorly executed. 

The texture problems in later sections of the game really are just not good and break you out of the game as soon as you see them. Also the frequent frame drops happen quite often in the end game section. Also the ending is very out of place and happens way too soon.

The game took me 3 hours to finish and I took my time off and explored the forest and not to mention I got lost quite a lot during my play time.

Alright here is the problem I had with the plot so *SPOILER WARNING*

Alright the two subplots with the missing girls and the stalker are very mediocre. First the missing girl subplot has one of the worst wraps up I have ever seen. The game sort of expects you that the stalker did something to them, but it later turns out that they were messing around somewhere else which I thought was cheap.

The stalker storyline has a very nice buildup, but the ending for the subplot felt very out of place and very weird with in tone of the rest of the game. Thinking you will end up with a satisfying conclusion the game lets you down right at the end.

*SPOILER WARNING OVER*

Overall, I enjoyed my time with Firewatch. While I don't think it's worth the full price at a discount I can safely say you can check this game out.

More art than game, Firewatch is one of those things you think about from time to time. Personally I think the story is gripping and definitely the strongest part. The art style is also incredible and plays to the strengths of the type of game it is. Go in blind if you can and replay it years later once you've forgotten most of the story. I saw a guide titled “How to cure depression after completing the game” and thought it would help. It didn’t.

Actually, finishing the game left me feeling hollow — not because it was bad, but because it hit somewhere deep and personal in a way I wasn’t prepared for.

It isn’t the greatest game I’ve ever played, but it’s definitely a very good one. There’s something undeniably captivating about it — the atmosphere, the visuals, the music, the voice acting — all of it works together to create a deeply immersive experience. The graphics are stunning; I often stopped just to admire the view and take a screenshot.

The story is linear, but it still gives small windows of freedom — the possibility to explore the forest beyond the main objectives, stumble upon little moments or places that make the world feel alive.

For me, it was depressing in a quiet, creeping way. It reflects some of the things I fear in real life. Still, I’m glad I played it. It’s a beautiful experience — not because of action or thrill, but because of its emotional depth and the way it lingers in your mind long after it’s over.

Firewatch is a first-person, narrative adventure game taking place on a stunning stretch of nature somewhere in the Wyoming wilderness. You play as Hank Henry, a newly designated fire lookout assigned to an outpost in the area, who’s also trying to flee a troubled past.

The introduction to the story is presented through a visual novel-esque format, allowing you to choose between two different paths which ultimately lead to the same destination. This section is interspersed with brief gameplay segments of Henry making his way to his new home away from home. 

Through this beginning sequence, we learn that he has a wife, Julia, who he met at a bar a long time ago. You witness their life together, through the good, the bad, and eventually the ugly. Before long, Julia is diagnosed with dementia, and soon her condition spirals out of control, with her family taking her back to her home in Australia to look after her.

Instead of sorting himself out and going to Australia to see her, he joins the firewatch service, placing him at Two Forks Lookout. This introduction is great for a couple of reasons. Firstly, it immediately sets the tone of the story, and gives you a pretty good grasp of the topics it’s going to cover. Secondly, it quickly provides valuable insight into who Henry is as a character, as well as his motivations for being where he is.

In all honesty, I could immediately relate to and sympathise with Henry. The game all but subtly plays into the escapist fantasy that I believe a lot of people share, - I know I certainly do - which is why I found myself fully invested in the narrative very early on. Sometimes a problem will feel so big, that all you’ll want to do is walk away; a choice that everyone has a right to. This is one of Firewatch’s most alluring facets, and it’s executed to such an exceptional degree. 

Despite being in the wilderness, you’re not quite alone. Enter Delilah, a knowledgeable, experienced fire lookout stationed in a nearby outpost, who acts as Henry’s supervisor. Through walkie-talkie communication, you’ll be reporting to her about pretty much anything of interest. This more or less sums up the first couple hours. It’s a slow start, but it serves as a way for the two of them to form a connection, of which is one of my favourite aspects of the game as a whole.

The authenticity of these characters cannot be understated. They feel like real people, thanks to their stellar writing and voice acting performances. Their motives are genuine and consistent, and even their smallest interactions feel like they have merit. It’s something that stays continuously great from start to finish. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2743822963

Which is why it really annoys me that the narrative ends the way it does. I don’t have a problem with the content of the conclusion, but the pace of it is completely out of left field. It’s a contrast that painfully conflicts with everything that came before it, and that I cannot help but think was written in a rushed manner.

How you experience this sequence can vary based on what dialogue options you pick. While Firewatch is very much linear, and does not stray from its set path at all, these options can give a sense of how Henry develops over time, but with the ones I picked, it didn’t really feel like he learnt anything at all after this. If given just a few more scenes, I’m certain that the ending could’ve felt less ham-fisted than it currently does. 

I will say this, it doesn’t ruin what comes before, at least not for me. The story as a whole has a lot to remember. It has charm, wit, intrigue, mystery, and suspense. I just wish there was more at the end. 

[h1]When the Sun is Down You Can Just… Get Lost...[/h1]

While the narrative may have a lot of depth, the gameplay has less to get sucked into, but I don’t mean that in a negative sense; quite the contrary actually. What appears superficial at first slowly begins to feel natural and fitting with the style of game it is.

In blanket terms, Firewatch is a walking simulator that provides you with a map and compass, then tells you where to go, but leaves it up to you to figure out how to get to your destination. Since you’re a fire watcher, you’re expected to maintain the area, making sure everything’s in good shape and isn’t on the verge of catching fire. 

You’ll sometimes be given a hint on how to get to a certain place, - go back to X, then head east - but it’s up to you to figure out the rest, and I loved that. Plotting and navigating your way around an area makes each trek feel engaging and challenging in their own way. It feels much less like a walking simulator in that respect.    

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2743817698

It helps that the place you are looking after is a treat for the eyes. The map is large and full of vistas to marvel at; screenshot lovers are in for a luxury here. The game’s fantastic use of colour makes each location you travel to a sight to behold.

Despite the narrative occasionally taking a creepy turn or two, exploring the wilderness is a rather relaxing activity. There’s so much to find, with plenty of things to talk to Delilah about, whether it be items in supply caches from previous lookouts, or various points of interest that have history or other interesting facts. It’s not something that will appeal to everyone, but I really liked it.   

If I had to make one slight complaint about the environment, it is that there isn’t really that much living in it. Where are all the animals? From memory, I found a deer, a raccoon, a tortoise, three ducks, and a few butterflies. Sometimes you can hear things rummaging through the bushes, but you can’t see anything. Just came across as strange.

[h1]In Conclusion[/h1]

Sitting at the heart of Firewatch is a deeply personal tale containing many relatable aspects. Despite having a bright, luscious appearance, it is not a happy experience, but it is filled with moments that will undoubtedly put a smile on your face.

While it didn’t conclude on the highest peak, the journey to it is something I wholeheartedly recommend. Its memorable characters, beautiful set pieces and charming gameplay make this a must-have for those looking for a great narrative experience. It’s a game that will stick with me for a while.

[h1]The Game[/h1]
A game that should only be played once. A game that discovers the problem of a normal human mind. A game that reflects our real world.

[h1]The Story[/h1]
The story this game tells is of guilt, sorrow and loss. This story can only be felt by interacting with it. This story can not be told by any other media. 

[h1]The Unsatisfactory Ending[/h1]
The ending if this game is so unsatisfactory that it pulls you out of itself to let you think about your own life. I play games to unwind and relax, to forget my own problems and struggles but this game just reflected that back to me. The thing from which I tried to run away was thrown back at me. There was no happy end to this story, yet it makes you feel at ease after completing. 

[h1]Final Thought[/h1]
Firewatch tells a story that has never been and will never be told by any other media. The story which connects our real lives to the lives of Henry and Delilah. The guilt felt by Ned is felt by the player. This game is too complex or rather I should say that the human mind is too complex to describe in words.

Firewatch is a wonderful story. On the surface about forgiveness, regret, the role of memories and of taking time out to reflect, and the importance of reaching out to others. Especially when you've got things you need to reach deep into yourself to consider, much of which remains undecided.

Under the surface though... [spoiler]Firewatch is a game about psychotic, manipulative, and possibly murderous cuckholdry.

"Delilah" manipulates through sultry and playful flirting knowing well that people take the job to escape and are likely easily malleable.

Delilah's other half (Javier - pretending to be "Ned") sets up the "scenes" and Delilah maintains contact from the tower to ensure that you're following the carrot like a good boy.

There is a point where Delilah "leaves" the broadcast button on while she's talking with "Ned" (Javier). Listen carefully to both the tone and context of this conversation because it sets the context for all the later pretense.

If you choose to go to the research outpost once you've retrieved the fire axe Delilah is instantly angry, then realizes that this situation can be easily dealt with - "Ned" fixes the research camp discovery shortly after you leave...

Again listen carefully to Delilah's tone here. She is speaking first to you (because you weren't being a good dog) then to "Them" (telling "Ned" to burn the camp down through fake anger).

Delilah's manipulation is crystal clear from the beginning if you're paying attention. Throughout the story she constantly convinces you that you are her only contact, your only life line, gets angry when you do the unexpected, and plays the victim in the end -- even plays off any odd behaviour as having had "a bit too much to drink".

All said Firewatch is a beautifully made game, with some very extreme undertones. The suspense is immediate, and constant.

I'm surprised that people haven't seen between the lines more here.

Whoever wrote the story is a Godsdamn genius.[/spoiler]
